citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Assume AC. Fix a finite-horizon model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] with
state and observation equations
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k\qquad (1\le k\le T),$$
where $X_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, the centered Gaussian noises $q_k,r_k$ are
mutually independent across times and from $X_0$, and $P_0,Q_k,R_k$ are
symmetric positive semidefinite. Let the parameters and observations be
admissible for [[alg-kalman-filter]], so the recursively formed innovation
covariances
$$S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k$$
are positive definite for every $1\le k\le T$. Run that algorithm from
$m_{0|0}=m_0$ and $P_{0|0}=P_0$. Then, for each $0\le k\le T$, the map
$$\pi_k(y_{1:k},\cdot)=N_{d_k}(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k}),P_{k|k})$$
is an everywhere-defined filtering kernel for $X_k$ given $Y_{1:k}$ in the
sense of [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]]. The empty history at $k=0$ is a
singleton, and $\pi_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$. In particular, these recursions
give an exact Gaussian conditional-law version at every observation history;
each $P_{k|k}$ is positive semidefinite. Singular initial, process,
measurement, predicted-state, and filtered-state covariances are allowed.
Equivalently, the covariance update can be written in Joseph form
$$P_{k|k}=(I-K_kH_k)P_{k|k-1}(I-K_kH_k)^T+K_kR_kK_k^T.$$
Only the innovation matrices being solved must be positive definite. No
pointwise uniqueness of a conditional-law version on null histories,
observation-density assumption, or numerical-stability claim is made.

Let $X,Y,Z$ be random elements with values in measurable spaces
$(E,\mathcal E)$, $(H,\mathcal H)$, and $(W,\mathcal W)$. Suppose $Z$ is
independent of the random element $(X,Y)$, and let
$\kappa:H\to E$ be a supplied conditional law of $X$ given $Y$. For each
$h\in H$, form the product probability
$\Lambda(h,\cdot)=\kappa(h,\cdot)\otimes\mathcal L(Z)$ on
$\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal W$. Then $\Lambda$ is a conditional law of
$(X,Z)$ given $Y$. If $\Phi:E\times W\to V$ is measurable into a measurable
space $(V,\mathcal V)$, then
$$\Lambda^\Phi(h,C):=\Lambda(h,\Phi^{-1}(C))$$
is a conditional law of $\Phi(X,Z)$ given $Y$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

Assume AC and fix a finite-horizon model of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]. There is a
probability space carrying mutually independent Gaussian vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ with the stated laws. The recursions
$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t$ and $y_t=H_t x_t+r_t$ induce the general kernel-product
law of [[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. In the interleaved order
$Z_T=(x_0,x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_T,y_T)$, there is a deterministic matrix $M_T$
such that
$$Z_T=M_T W_T,\qquad W_T=(x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T),$$
and
$$Z_T\sim N\!\left(M_T a_T,\ M_T\Sigma_T M_T^T\right),\qquad a_T=(m_0,0,\ldots,0),\quad \Sigma_T=\operatorname{diag}(P_0,Q_1,R_1,\ldots,Q_T,R_T).$$
The covariance may be singular.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume AC and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ with a state-space model by
probability kernels as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. If $T=0$, put $\Omega_T=E_0$;
otherwise put $\Omega_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times
F_T$. Let $\mathcal Z_T$ be the corresponding finite-product sigma-algebra
and write $(\Omega_T,\mathcal Z_T,P_T)$ for its finite-horizon probability
space. The law $P_T$ is the unique law supplied by
[[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]]. Let $X_t$ and
$Y_t$ be the coordinate random elements taking values in $E_t$ and $F_t$. For
$t\ge1$, write $Y_{1:t}:=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)$ and
$\mathsf F_{1:t}:=F_1\times\cdots\times F_t$ with its finite-product
sigma-algebra; let $\mathsf F_{1:0}$ be a singleton and $Y_{1:0}$ its constant
map. The factors are standard Borel, meaning measurably isomorphic to Polish
spaces ([[def-standard-borel-space]]), and their finite products are standard
Borel ([[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

The **initial filtering kernel** $\pi_0:\mathsf F_{1:0}\to E_0$ assigns
$\mu_0$ to the unique empty history; it is the conditional law of $X_0$ given
the trivial history. For $1\le t\le T$, a **filtering kernel at time $t$** is
a probability kernel $\pi_t:\mathsf F_{1:t}\to E_t$ such that
$\omega\mapsto\pi_t(Y_{1:t}(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional
distribution of $X_t$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:t})$. For $1\le t\le T$, a
**predictive kernel at time $t$** is a probability kernel
$\pi_{t|t-1}:\mathsf F_{1:t-1}\to E_t$ whose composition with $Y_{1:t-1}$
is a regular conditional distribution of $X_t$ given
$\sigma(Y_{1:t-1})$. A **finite-horizon smoothing kernel** is a probability
kernel $\psi_T:\mathsf F_{1:T}\to E_0\times\cdots\times E_T$ whose
composition with $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular conditional distribution of the full
state path $(X_0,\ldots,X_T)$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Here a regular
conditional distribution is an everywhere probability kernel satisfying the
conditional event identities in
[[def-regular-conditional-distribution]], and a conditional law given a
random element is its data-indexed kernel form in
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]].

These kernels are versions: their values can be changed on a measurable set
of observation histories of probability zero without changing the conditional
identities. No density is assumed in these definitions. The state-space model
here is one fixed law. A parametric statistical model is instead a map
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$ from a parameter set to probability laws; its
measurability is not asserted without a parameter sigma-algebra
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: Fix a history $h=y_{1:k}$. By [F3], the conditional law of $X_k$ is $N(m_{k|k}(h),P_{k|k})$. The next process noise is independent of the past by [F1], so [F4] extends this filtering kernel by $q_{k+1}$ and pushes it forward through $(x,q)\mapsto(x,F_{k+1}x+q)$. By [F5], $(X_k,q_{k+1})$ is jointly Gaussian, and the projection characterization in [F10] makes its linear image $(X_k,X_{k+1})$ jointly Gaussian. Its mean is $(m_{k|k},F_{k+1}m_{k|k})$, its state covariance is $P_{k|k}$, its cross-covariance is $P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^T$, and its next-state covariance is $P_{k+1|k}$. The latter block is positive definite by hypothesis. Apply [F6] with that observed block: the conditional mean and covariance are exactly the displayed $Q_k$ parameters, so $V_k\succeq0$. The history mean is affine by [F2], and representing each Gaussian section as a translate of fixed $N(0,V_k)$ plus [F8] gives joint measurability in $(h,x_{k+1})$. Thus $Q_k$ is an everywhere probability kernel.

Write $H=Y_{1:k}$, $V=X_{k+1}$, and $Z=Y_{k+1:T}$. By [F7], the full path law factors by taking the law of $(H,X_k)$, applying the transition kernel at $k+1$, and then a future observation kernel $R(V,dz)$ formed by the remaining transition and observation kernels. The first two factors disintegrate as $\pi_k(h,dx_k)K_{k+1}(x_k,dv)=\rho_k(h,dv)Q_k(h,v,dx_k)$ by step 1.1, where $\rho_k$ is the one-step predictive law. Substitution gives the joint factorization as the law of $H$ followed by $\rho_k$, $Q_k$, and $R$. The future kernel depends on the past only through $V$, and its iterated integrals are measurable by [F8].

For any Borel set $A$ of $X_k$ and any Borel set $D$ in the product space of $(H,V,Z)$, integrate $1_A(x_k)1_D(h,v,z)$ in the factorization from step 2.1. This gives $\mathbb P(X_k\in A,(H,V,Z)\in D)=\int_D Q_k(h,v,A)\,\mathbb P_{(H,V,Z)}(dh,dv,dz)$. This is the RCD event identity for $Q_k$ given $(H,V,Z)$; its kernel properties were established in step 1.1. Since $(H,Z)=Y_{1:T}$, it is also a version of the conditional law given $(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})$. The factorization uses model kernels rather than observation densities, and the only inverse is of $P_{k+1|k}\succ0$.

boundaries.reason: The lemma assumes k<T and positive finite-dimensional state and observation dimensions.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 uses only P_{k+1|k}≻0; no zero or singular forecast is inverted.
Step 1.1 constructs an everywhere conditional kernel for every next-state value.
Step 1.1 permits singular P_{k|k}, Q_{k+1}, and V_k when the forecast remains SPD.
Statement and step 2.1 include k=0 and k=T−1; the past or future history may be empty.
Statement A1 records AC through the Gaussian suppliers; step 1.1 introduces no stronger choice.

states $X_0,\ldots,X_T$, observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_T$, and Borel observation
space $\mathsf Y_{1:T}=\mathbb R^{p_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^{p_T}$,
with the empty product a singleton when $T=0$.
For $0\le k\le T$, a **fixed-interval smoothing kernel for $X_k$** is an
everywhere-defined probability kernel
$$\psi_{k|T}:\mathsf Y_{1:T}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d_k}$$
whose composition with the full observation vector $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular
conditional distribution of $X_k$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Thus it is the
single-time marginal smoothing law after all observations through time $T$
are supplied. The full-path smoothing kernel and its version convention are
defined in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]].

This definition does not assert that such a kernel exists or is unique at
observation values in a null set. The theorem on this page constructs a
Gaussian version under its explicit forecast and innovation assumptions.

Assume AC. Let $(X_0,\ldots,X_T,Y_1,\ldots,Y_T)$ follow a finite-horizon
linear-Gaussian model as in
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]. Suppose
the Kalman filter of [[alg-kalman-filter]] is admissible: every innovation
covariance $S_j$ it solves is positive definite. Fix $0\le k<T$, and let
$m_{k|k},P_{k|k}$ and $m_{k+1|k},P_{k+1|k}$ be the corresponding filtered
and one-step predicted quantities. Assume in addition that
$P_{k+1|k}\succ0$. Put
$$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1},\qquad V_k=P_{k|k}-C_kP_{k+1|k}C_k^T.$$
Then $V_k\succeq0$, and the formula
$$Q_k(y_{1:k},x_{k+1},\cdot)=N\!\left(m_{k|k}(y_{1:k})+C_k(x_{k+1}-m_{k+1|k}(y_{1:k})),V_k\right)$$
defines an everywhere probability kernel. It is a conditional law of $X_k$
given $(Y_{1:k},X_{k+1})$ and also a version of the conditional law of
$X_k$ given $(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})$ under the full finite-horizon model. Thus
future observations do not change this backward kernel once $X_{k+1}$ is
also given. The inverse is the ordinary inverse of the positive-definite
forecast covariance; no singular-forecast extension is asserted.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: At time $T$, the conditioning data for the forward filter are exactly $y_{1:T}$. By [F3], the terminal filter kernel $N(m_{T|T},P_{T|T})$ is an everywhere conditional-law version of $X_T$ given these data, with $P_{T|T}\succeq0$. It is therefore the base case for the fixed-interval smoothing kernels in [F4].

Suppose the Gaussian kernel $\psi_{k+1|T}(y,\cdot)$ is an RCD of $X_{k+1}$ given $Y_{1:T}=y$. Define $\psi_{k|T}(y,A)=\int Q_k(y_{1:k},x,A)\,\psi_{k+1|T}(y,dx)$ for each Borel state set $A$. This is a probability kernel by [F5]–[F6]. To verify its RCD identity, define $\nu(D)=\int\!\int 1_D(y,x)\,\psi_{k+1|T}(y,dx)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy)$ for Borel $D$ in the product of data and state spaces. Measurability follows from [F6]; for pairwise disjoint $D_n$, monotone convergence gives countable additivity, and $\nu$ has total mass one. Its rectangle values equal those of the actual joint law of $(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})$ by the RCD identity for $\psi_{k+1|T}$. By [F8], the measures agree on every Borel set. Thus for any Borel data set $B$ and state set $A$, $\int_B\psi_{k|T}(y,A)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy)=\int_{B\times\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}}Q_k(y_{1:k},x,A)\,\mathbb P_{(Y_{1:T},X_{k+1})}(dy,dx)=\mathbb P(X_k\in A,Y_{1:T}\in B)$, where the last equality is [F5] applied to the conditioning event $B\times\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}$. Hence $\psi_{k|T}$ is the required RCD.

Write $V_k=P_{k|k}-C_kP_{k+1|k}C_k^T$ as in [F5]. On the product probability space carrying independent $U\sim N(0,V_k)$ and $W\sim N(m_{k+1|T},P_{k+1|T})$, the integral in step 2.1 is the law of $m_{k|k}+C_k(W-m_{k+1|k})+U$ by [F9]. The covariance matrices of $U$ and $W$ are positive semidefinite by [F5] and the induction hypothesis, so both Gaussian laws exist by [A1, F11]. The product coordinates are independent by [F12]; [F10] makes their stack jointly Gaussian, and its affine image is Gaussian by the projection characterization in [F11]. Independence makes the cross-covariance terms vanish, so its mean is $m_{k|k}+C_k(m_{k+1|T}-m_{k+1|k})$ and its covariance is $V_k+C_kP_{k+1|T}C_k^T=P_{k|k}+C_k(P_{k+1|T}-P_{k+1|k})C_k^T$. This is exactly the smoother update in the statement and algorithm. The first covariance expression is positive semidefinite, so the updated covariance is positive semidefinite as well.

Starting from step 1.1, apply steps 2.1–3.1 for $k=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$. The induction constructs an everywhere smoothing kernel at each time and identifies its mean and covariance with the algorithm output. When $T=0$ only the base case is needed. Positive definiteness is used only for the forecast inverses in [F5] and the forward innovation solves in [F2]; no singular forecast is inverted.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, positive state dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_T$,
and positive observation dimensions $p_1,\ldots,p_T$. The input is a
linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]], with
matrices $F_k\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_{k-1}}$ and
$H_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k\times d_k}$, initial mean $m_0$, and symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariances $P_0,Q_k,R_k$. Its state and observation
equations are
$$X_k=F_kX_{k-1}+q_k,\qquad Y_k=H_kX_k+r_k,$$
where $q_k\sim N(0,Q_k)$ and $r_k\sim N(0,R_k)$ are centered and mutually
independent across all times and of $X_0$.

The admissible data are vectors $y_k\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$ for which every
innovation covariance encountered below is positive definite. Positive
definite means $u^TS_ku>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^{p_k}$. The
algorithm returns predicted and updated means and covariances and the
innovation and gain at each time. Initialize
$$m_{0|0}=m_0,\qquad P_{0|0}=P_0.$$
For $k=1,\ldots,T$, perform:

1. Predict:
$$m_{k|k-1}=F_km_{k-1|k-1},\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F_kP_{k-1|k-1}F_k^T+Q_k.$$
2. Form the innovation and its covariance:
$$v_k=y_k-H_km_{k|k-1},\qquad S_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}H_k^T+R_k.$$
3. Factor $S_k=L_kL_k^T$ with lower-triangular $L_k$ having positive
diagonal, using
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Solve $L_kU_k=H_kP_{k|k-1}$ and $L_k^TK_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. This
defines $K_k^T=S_k^{-1}H_kP_{k|k-1}$, hence
$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] and data
$y_{1:T}$ for which [[alg-kalman-filter]] is admissible. Its forward output
contains filtered means and covariances $m_{k|k},P_{k|k}$ and predicted means
and covariances $m_{k+1|k},P_{k+1|k}$. Assume each forecast covariance used
below is positive definite, meaning $u^TP_{k+1|k}u>0$ for every nonzero
$u\in\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}$. Positive semidefinite means the same quadratic
form is nonnegative for every $u$.

The algorithm takes that forward output as input, initializes
$$m_{T|T}:=m_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}},\qquad P_{T|T}:=P_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}}$$
and for $k=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$ performs the following steps:

1. Form the backward gain
$$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1}.$$
For the computation, factor $P_{k+1|k}=L_kL_k^T$ with the unique
positive-diagonal Cholesky factor from
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]],
then solve $L_kU_k=F_{k+1}P_{k|k}$ and
$L_k^TC_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. Thus no inverse is formed in the
procedure.
2. Update the smoothed mean and covariance:
$$m_{k|T}=m_{k|k}+C_k(m_{k+1|T}-m_{k+1|k})$$
$$P_{k|T}=P_{k|k}+C_k(P_{k+1|T}-P_{k+1|k})C_k^T$$

Return $(m_{k|T},P_{k|T})_{k=0}^T$. For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the
output is the initial filtered pair. The algorithm is undefined if a
forecast covariance to be solved is singular; it makes no pseudoinverse,
complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim. The theorem on
this page proves that the outputs are moments of the fixed-interval
conditional laws under these hypotheses.

Assume AC and fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian model
([[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]) with
$P_0,Q_j,R_j\succeq0$. Run the forward Kalman filter on data $y_{1:T}$,
with every innovation covariance $S_j$ positive definite. Also assume that
every one-step forecast covariance $P_{k+1|k}$ is positive definite for
$0\le k<T$. Let $(m_{k|T},P_{k|T})_{k=0}^T$ be the output of
[[alg-rauch-tung-striebel-smoother]] applied to that forward output. Then,
for every $0\le k\le T$,
$$N_{d_k}(m_{k|T}(y_{1:T}),P_{k|T})$$
is an everywhere-defined fixed-interval smoothing kernel for $X_k$ in the
sense of [[def-fixed-interval-gaussian-smoothing-law]]. In particular,
$P_{k|T}\succeq0$. Singular initial, process, measurement, filtered, and
smoothed covariances are allowed; only the innovation matrices solved by the
filter and the forecast matrices inverted by this smoother must be positive
definite. The formulas select a conditional-law version at every data value;
other versions may differ on a set of observation data of probability zero.
No pseudoinverse result for a singular forecast is asserted.

derivations.claim: The first backward gain is $C_1=(2/3)/(5/3)=2/5$. Therefore $m_{1|2}=2/3+(2/5)(3/2-2/3)=1$ and $P_{1|2}=2/3+(2/5)(5/8-5/3)(2/5)=1/2$. The next gain is $C_0=1/2$, so $m_{0|2}=0+(1/2)(1-0)=1/2$ and $P_{0|2}=1+(1/2)(1/2-2)(1/2)=5/8$. The theorem [F4] identifies the resulting smoothing kernels as $N(1/2,5/8)$ for $X_0$, $N(1,1/2)$ for $X_1$, and $N(3/2,5/8)$ for $X_2$ at the selected data history.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 and step 2.1 compute S_1=3 and S_2=8/3, both positive.
Step 3.1 applies the exact smoothing theorem to normalized Gaussian laws.
The example uses strictly positive prior and noise variances, so degeneracy is not part of this example.
Steps 1.1–3.1 cover the two forward times and backward steps k=1,0.
Statement A1 supplies the Gaussian-law convention; steps 1.1–3.1 use only finite exact arithmetic.

$K_k=P_{k|k-1}H_k^TS_k^{-1}$, without explicitly forming $S_k^{-1}$.
4. Update:
$$m_{k|k}=m_{k|k-1}+K_kv_k,\qquad P_{k|k}=P_{k|k-1}-K_kS_kK_k^T.$$

For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the returned pair is $(m_0,P_0)$. No
inverse of $P_0$, $Q_k$, or $R_k$ is used. This item defines the procedure
and makes no complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim.

Fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian model from
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]] and data
$y_{1:T}$ for which [[alg-kalman-filter]] is admissible. Its forward output
contains filtered means and covariances $m_{k|k},P_{k|k}$ and predicted means
and covariances $m_{k+1|k},P_{k+1|k}$. Assume each forecast covariance used
below is positive definite, meaning $u^TP_{k+1|k}u>0$ for every nonzero
$u\in\mathbb R^{d_{k+1}}$. Positive semidefinite means the same quadratic
form is nonnegative for every $u$.

The algorithm takes that forward output as input, initializes
$$m_{T|T}:=m_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}},\qquad P_{T|T}:=P_{T|T}^{\mathrm{filter}}$$
and for $k=T-1,T-2,\ldots,0$ performs the following steps:

1. Form the backward gain
$$C_k=P_{k|k}F_{k+1}^TP_{k+1|k}^{-1}.$$
For the computation, factor $P_{k+1|k}=L_kL_k^T$ with the unique
positive-diagonal Cholesky factor from
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]],
then solve $L_kU_k=F_{k+1}P_{k|k}$ and
$L_k^TC_k^T=U_k$ by triangular solves. Thus no inverse is formed in the
procedure.
2. Update the smoothed mean and covariance:
$$m_{k|T}=m_{k|k}+C_k(m_{k+1|T}-m_{k+1|k})$$
$$P_{k|T}=P_{k|k}+C_k(P_{k+1|T}-P_{k+1|k})C_k^T$$

Return $(m_{k|T},P_{k|T})_{k=0}^T$. For $T=0$ the loop is empty and the
output is the initial filtered pair. The algorithm is undefined if a
forecast covariance to be solved is singular; it makes no pseudoinverse,
complexity, rounding-error, or numerical-stability claim. The theorem on
this page proves that the outputs are moments of the fixed-interval
conditional laws under these hypotheses.

Assume AC and fix a finite-horizon linear-Gaussian state-space model
([[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]) with
states $X_0,\ldots,X_T$, observations $Y_1,\ldots,Y_T$, and Borel observation
space $\mathsf Y_{1:T}=\mathbb R^{p_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^{p_T}$,
with the empty product a singleton when $T=0$.
For $0\le k\le T$, a **fixed-interval smoothing kernel for $X_k$** is an
everywhere-defined probability kernel
$$\psi_{k|T}:\mathsf Y_{1:T}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d_k}$$
whose composition with the full observation vector $Y_{1:T}$ is a regular
conditional distribution of $X_k$ given $\sigma(Y_{1:T})$. Thus it is the
single-time marginal smoothing law after all observations through time $T$
are supplied. The full-path smoothing kernel and its version convention are
defined in [[def-state-space-filtering-laws]].

This definition does not assert that such a kernel exists or is unique at
observation values in a null set. The theorem on this page constructs a
Gaussian version under its explicit forecast and innovation assumptions.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $X_0=0$ and $q_1=0$ almost surely, so $X_1=0$ almost surely. The observation is $Y_1=r_1$ and the model covariances are positive semidefinite.

The forward recursion gives $P_{1|0}=1\cdot0\cdot1+0=0$ and $m_{1|0}=0$. Since $H_1=0$ and $R_1=1$, its innovation covariance is $S_1=1>0$, gain $K_1=0$, and filtered state remains $N(0,0)$. Thus the forward filter is admissible, while the RTS step would require the ordinary inverse of $P_{1|0}=0$, which does not exist by [F4]. No pseudoinverse substitution follows from that algorithm.

Define $\psi_{0|1}(y,\cdot)=\delta_0$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$. For any Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\mathbb P(X_0\in A,Y_1\in B)=1_{\{0\in A\}}\mathbb P(Y_1\in B)=\int_B\delta_0(A)\,\mathbb P_{Y_1}(dy)$ by step 1.1. Hence this everywhere-defined kernel satisfies the RCD identity in [F5]; it is the fixed-interval smoothing law even though the ordinary RTS recursion is undefined.
